The first click shows both grey baseline bars and b labels; the second adds the blue memory segment only to old. Bar heights are schematic, not parameter estimates. Activation supports a choice; a is not a storage probability. ::: ## Choice probabilities: Luce’s choice rule {#simple-choice-rule auto-animate=true} :::: {.columns .m3-choice-layout} ::: {.column width="45%"} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: {.column .m3-choice-formulas width="55%"} ::: {.fragment fragment-index=0} $$ P(\mathrm{old})= \frac{b+a}{(b+a)+b} $$ ::: ::: {.fragment fragment-index=1} $$ P(\mathrm{new})= \frac{b}{(b+a)+b} $$ ::: ::: :::: ::: {.notes} Reference: Oberauer & Lewandowsky (2019), Eq. 2, applied to this teaching recognition example. Normalize the activation values directly: old receives b+a, new receives b. Point to each contribution in the shared denominator. This rule uses nonnegative activation values with a positive total; a fixed positive baseline sets their scale. The original paper fixed b at 0.1. ::: ## Choice probabilities: Softmax {#softmax-choice-rule auto-animate=true} :::: {.columns .m3-choice-layout} ::: {.column width="45%"} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: {.column .m3-choice-formulas width="55%"} ::: {.fragment fragment-index=0} $$ P(\mathrm{old})= \frac{\exp(b+a)}{\exp(b+a)+\exp(b)} $$ ::: ::: {.fragment fragment-index=1} $$ P(\mathrm{new})= \frac{\exp(b)}{\exp(b+a)+\exp(b)} $$ ::: ::: :::: ::: {.notes} Choice-rule reference: Oberauer (2023), Eq. 4. Now transform the same activations with exp before normalizing. These are alternative choice rules with different parameter scales, not equivalent rewritings of one model. Use softmax in all subsequent examples. Point from each numerator to the corresponding image on the preceding slide. Both options compete in the same choice and share a denominator. Their probabilities sum to one. A common b cancels from softmax; keep it visible to explain activation sources rather than estimating it independently. ::: ## Memory activation and choice probabilities {#stronger-item-memory-favors-the-old-image .m3-figure} ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](02_M3_files/figure-revealjs/recognition-demo-1.png){fig-alt='Illustrative softmax probabilities: old and new are equally likely when memory activation is zero; greater memory activation favors old.' width=960} ::: ::: ## Two dimensions of memory strength {.section-divider} **Item memory** and **binding memory** as sources of activation. ## Example of a location memory task {#location-memory-ready data-autoslide="0" data-transition="none" .m3-task-slide} ```{=html}

The pictures disappear as the next appears. Change only the spatial association and the retrieval instruction, not the basic presentation logic. These intervals are for the teaching demonstration. ::: ## Example of a location memory task {#which-image-was-in-the-center data-autoslide="0" data-transition="none" .m3-task-slide} ```{=html}

The test contains one correct image, one other studied image, and one new image. ::: ## Item and binding activation {#three-options-reveal-two-memory-sources .m3-binding-slide auto-animate=true} :::: {.m3-binding-layout} ::: {.m3-binding-diagram} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: {.m3-binding-formula .fragment fragment-index=3} $$ \begin{aligned} A(\mathrm{correct}) &= b + a + c \\ A(\mathrm{other}) &= b + a \\ A(\mathrm{new}) &= b \end{aligned} $$ ::: :::: ::: {.notes} Start with axes and options only. The first click shows the three grey baseline bars and b labels; the second adds item activation a to both studied images; the third adds orange binding c only to the cued image. Do not add total labels above the bars. The sources follow Oberauer & Lewandowsky (2019), Eq. 1; this task is a teaching example. ::: ## Memory activation and choice probabilities {#what-does-binding-add .m3-figure} ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](02_M3_files/figure-revealjs/binding-demo-1.png){fig-alt='Illustrative predictions holding item activation fixed: correct and other are equally likely without binding; adding binding increases correct choices.' width=960} ::: ::: ::: {.notes} These are illustrative predictions with fixed a. Without binding, correct and other have equal activation; increasing c favors correct. ::: ## Applying M3 to simple span {.section-divider} Estimating item and binding memory with bmm. ## Example of a simple-span task {#simple-span-ready data-autoslide="0" data-transition="none" .m3-task-slide} ```{=html}

``` ## Specifying the simple-span model {#specify-categories-and-their-option-counts .smaller .m3-model-slide} [[specify]{.on} · fit · evaluate]{.track} ::::: {.m3-model-content} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-line-numbers="1-7|2|3|4|5|6"} model_simple <- m3( resp_cats = c("corr", "other", "npl"), num_options = c("n_corr", "n_other", "n_npl"), version = "ss", choice_rule = "softmax", links = list(a = "identity", c = "identity") ) ``` ::: ```{=html} ``` :::: {.m3-model-explanations} ::: {.fragment .current-visible fragment-index=0} `resp_cats`: observed response counts for Correct, Others, and NPL. ::: ::: {.fragment .current-visible fragment-index=1} `num_options`: available options in the same category order. ::: ::: {.fragment .current-visible fragment-index=2} `version`: `"ss"` = simple span · `"cs"` = complex span · `"custom"` = custom model. ::: ::: {.fragment .current-visible fragment-index=3} `choice_rule`: `"simple"` = Luce’s choice rule · `"softmax"` = exponential choice weights. ::: ::: {.fragment fragment-index=4} ::::: {.fragment .fade-out fragment-index=7} `links`: map regression predictors to parameter values. :::: {.columns} ::: {.column .fragment width="33%" fragment-index=4} ### identity ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](02_M3_files/figure-revealjs/link-identity-1.png){fig-alt='Identity inverse link: parameter value equals the regression predictor, including negative values.' width=100%} ::: ::: ::: ::: {.column .fragment width="33%" fragment-index=5} ### log ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](02_M3_files/figure-revealjs/link-log-1.png){fig-alt='Log inverse link: exponentiating the regression predictor produces positive parameter values.' width=100%} ::: ::: ::: ::: {.column .fragment width="33%" fragment-index=6} ### logit ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](02_M3_files/figure-revealjs/link-logit-1.png){fig-alt='Logit inverse link: a logistic curve maps the regression predictor to parameter values between zero and one.' width=100%} ::: ::: ::: :::: ::::: ::: ::: {.fragment fragment-index=7} :::: {.columns .m3-choice-comparison} ::: {.column .m3-choice-panel width="100%"} ### simple ::: {.m3-choice-equation} $$ P(k)=\frac{n_k A_k}{\sum_j n_j A_j} $$ ```{=html}
Cannot be negative
``` ::: ::: ::: {.column .m3-choice-panel width="100%"} ### softmax ::: {.m3-choice-equation} $$ P(k)=\frac{n_k\exp(A_k)}{\sum_j n_j\exp(A_j)} $$ ```{=html}
Can be negative
``` ::: ::: :::: ::: :::: ::::: ::: {.notes} Initially show the complete code without dimmed lines or explanations. Each click highlights the next parameter and shows its explanation together: resp_cats, num_options, version, then choice_rule. Valid options were checked against the installed bmm 1.3.1 m3 constructor. The native Quarto line-highlight plugin uses the code's initial fragment index to align its cloned steps. The conceptual b remains in teaching formulas. The implementation fixes the common baseline for identification; it cancels from softmax. Only a and c need regression formulas. Do not present b as a third estimable parameter. ::: ## Specifying parameter formulas {#specify-how-do-a-and-c-vary .smaller} [[specify]{.on} · fit · evaluate]{.track} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-line-numbers="true"} formula_simple <- bmf( c ~ 0 + ss_fac + (0 + ss_fac | id), a ~ 0 + ss_fac + (0 + ss_fac | id) ) ``` ::: ::: {.incremental} - `0 + ss_fac`: a separate mean for each **set size**. - `(0 + ss_fac | id)`: correlated participant deviations at each set size. ::: ::: {.notes} ss_fac treats set size as categorical. Both fixed and participant effects use one coefficient per set size, without a separate intercept. The fit uses only open-set data. The vertical bar retains correlations between each participant's deviations at different set sizes. ::: ## Setting priors: simple {#setting-priors-simple .smaller} [[specify]{.on} · fit · evaluate]{.track} **Log link:** priors on the log-activation scale. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} coefs <- paste0("ss_fac", c(2, 4, 6, 8)) priors_simple_rule <- c( set_prior("normal(1, 0.5)", nlpar = "a", coef = coefs), set_prior("normal(1.5, 0.5)", nlpar = "c", coef = coefs) ) ``` ::: These priors apply to the set-size means of log activation. The log link keeps $a$ and $c$ positive. ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](02_M3_files/figure-revealjs/prior-simple-density-1.png){fig-alt='Priors for a and c: normal densities on the link scale and their lognormal densities on the original scale, shown in blue and orange.' width=100%} ::: ::: ## Setting priors: softmax {#setting-priors-softmax .smaller} [[specify]{.on} · fit · evaluate]{.track} **Identity link:** priors on the activation scale. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} coefs <- paste0("ss_fac", c(2, 4, 6, 8)) priors_softmax <- c( set_prior("normal(3, 1)", nlpar = "a", coef = coefs), set_prior("normal(3, 1)", nlpar = "c", coef = coefs) ) ``` ::: These priors apply to the set-size means of activation. They are the priors used in this workshop fit. ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](02_M3_files/figure-revealjs/prior-softmax-density-1.png){fig-alt='Priors for a and c are both Normal(3, 1); link-scale and original-scale densities are identical under the identity link. The blue solid and orange dashed curves coincide.' width=100%} ::: ::: ## Fitting M3 with bmm {#fit-once-load-the-result-for-the-workshop .smaller .m3-model-slide} [specify · [fit]{.on} · evaluate]{.track} ::::: {.m3-model-content} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-line-numbers="true"} fit_simple <- bmm( formula = formula_simple, model = model_simple, data = dat_simple, prior = priors_softmax, chains = 4, cores = 4, iter = 5000, warmup = 2000, control = list(adapt_delta = 0.95), sample_prior = "yes", backend = "cmdstanr", seed = 2026 ) ``` ::: The sampling arguments work the same way as in the SDT model. ::::: ## Model fit: Observed and predicted responses {#evaluate-does-m3-reproduce-the-responses .smaller .m3-figure} [specify · fit · [evaluate]{.on}]{.track} `posterior_epred(fit_simple)` predicts counts in **all three categories**. ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](../data/figures/m3_simple_predictive.png){fig-alt='Observed and predicted open-set response proportions, with participant-level standard errors, across three categories.' width=100%} ::: ::: ::: {.notes} Compare observed and predicted means, including both error categories. Error bars are ±1 participant-level SE, not posterior predictive intervals. Close mean curves do not establish that every aspect of fit is adequate. ::: ## Parameter estimates: Item and binding memory {#interpret-item-memory-and-binding-memory .smaller .m3-figure} [specify · fit · [evaluate]{.on}]{.track} ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](../data/figures/m3_simple_parameters.png){fig-alt='Open-set item and binding memory medians and 95 percent credible intervals across set sizes, in blue and orange facets on a 0 to 6 activation scale.' width=100%} ::: ::: ::: {.small} Posterior medians and 95% credible intervals; parameters are on the activation scale. ::: ::: {.notes} Binding estimates have lower posterior medians at larger set sizes in the open set. Describe item-memory patterns separately rather than treating accuracy as a single memory parameter. These are model-based estimates under the chosen activation and choice rules. ::: ## Extending M3 to complex span {.section-divider} How does M3 account for distractor activation? ## Example of a complex-span task {#complex-span-instructions .m3-task-slide} ```{=html}

Which object is larger?

Remember the object inside the white circle and its color.

Use the mouse to click the object that is larger in real life.

``` ## Example of a complex-span task {#complex-span-ready data-autoslide="0" data-transition="none" .m3-task-slide} ```{=html}
``` ::: {.notes} Simplified complex-span demonstration based on Li, Frischkorn, and Oberauer (2026), Experiment 1. Press next to begin. The published arrow cue is replaced by a circular outline here as a simplified teaching display. The white ring appears with the pair and selects the memorandum during processing. It has a white outline and no fill. Both objects share a context color; processing requires selecting the larger object in real life. The target is designated before the size judgment. This example and the fitted application both use the pre-cue condition. ::: ## Example of a complex-span task {#targets-and-distractors .m3-timed data-autoslide="0" data-transition="none" .m3-task-slide} ```{=html}

Which object is larger?

Which object is larger?

Which object is larger?

``` ::: {.notes} This simplified display is presenter-paced. The white ring and the two objects appear simultaneously. Press next (or click an object) to show the following pair directly. After the last pair, press next to open the test. No blank stages or automatic timers remain. The original experiment allowed up to 2500 ms for processing and a 1500-ms post-processing interval; this demonstration does not reproduce those durations, record responses, or score choices. Each target/distractor pair differs by at least two levels in the authors' size ratings: image5/image1 = 4/2, image8/image2 = 4/2, and image24/image4 = 6/2. The targets are avocado, flamingo, croissant. The first and third targets are the smaller objects; the second is the larger object. The size-judgment question still asks for the larger object in every pair. Three context colors follow the published hue spacing. Original silhouettes are from the public OSF materials. The stimuli are a teaching selection, not the particular trial in Figure 1. ::: ## Example of a complex-span task {#five-response-categories data-autoslide="0" data-transition="none" .m3-task-slide auto-animate=true} ```{=html}
``` ::: {.notes} The color cue probes flamingo, not a spatial location or pair index. The 12 choices are 1 correct, 1 same-color distractor, 2 other targets, 2 other distractors, and 6 NPLs. The response categories are introduced on the following slide after the audience has selected a response. In the experiment each of the three colors was probed in randomized order with a 10-second response deadline; the slide shows one test and remains until the presenter advances. White silhouettes, context cue and two simultaneous objects match the published design; this is a reconstruction using original assets, not an archived screenshot. Source: Li et al. (2026), Experiment 1, Figure 1; doi:10.1037/xlm0001585. ::: ## Response categories and counts {#complex-response-categories .m3-complex-category-slide auto-animate=true} ```{=html}
Correct（1）：
Paired distractor（1）：
Other targets（2）：
Other distractors（2）：
NPL（6）：
``` ::: {.notes} The preceding test screen shrinks to the left; the five response categories appear on successive keypresses on the right. The purple context probes flamingo. Counts are 1 correct, 1 paired distractor (banana), 2 other targets (avocado, croissant), 2 other distractors (crocodile, octopus), and 6 NPLs. The screen retains the same option identities, ordering, and color cue. ::: ## Distractor activation and filtering {#filtering .m3-binding-slide} :::: {.m3-binding-layout} ::: {.m3-binding-diagram} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: {.m3-binding-formula .m3-category-activations .fragment fragment-index=4} $$ \begin{aligned} A(\mathrm{correct}) &= b + a + c \\ A(\mathrm{paired\ distractor}) &= b + f a + f c \\ A(\mathrm{other\ targets}) &= b + a \\ A(\mathrm{other\ distractors}) &= b + f a \\ A(\mathrm{NPL}) &= b \end{aligned} $$ ::: :::: ::: {.notes} The bars show one representative option per category. Start with axes and options only. First show baseline b, then item activation a, then binding activation c on three separate clicks. The fourth click illustrates filtering with f=0.5. Baseline is unchanged. Both distractor item and binding contributions are retained at 50% in the standard cs model. Original bar heights are preserved: removed portions are outlined with dashed borders and 20% fill opacity; solid portions show fa and fc. Filtering reduces each solid segment from its top down over 0.5 seconds, while the removed portion expands down from its original top. This shared multiplier is a model assumption, not a universal claim about filtering. f=0 leaves baseline alone. Bar heights and f=0.5 are teaching values, not fitted results. A larger c in the illustration is not an invariant property. See tutorial pp. 20–22 for the activation formulas. Show the activation decomposition for each response category on the final click. Each formula is activation per option, not a category probability. The same f scales item and binding activation for distractors in the standard bmm complex-span model. ::: ## Specifying the complex-span model {#extend-the-model-keep-the-workflow .smaller} [[specify]{.on} · fit · evaluate]{.track} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} model_complex <- m3( resp_cats = c("corr", "distc", "other", "disto", "npl"), num_options = c("n_corr", "n_distc", "n_other", "n_disto", "n_npl"), version = "cs", choice_rule = "softmax" ) formula_complex <- bmf( c ~ 1 + (1 | participant), a ~ 1 + (1 | participant), f ~ 1 + (1 | participant) ) ``` ::: ## Model fit: Observed and predicted responses {#evaluate-complex-span-fit .smaller .m3-figure} [specify · fit · [evaluate]{.on}]{.track} ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](../data/figures/m3_complex_predictive.png){fig-alt='Observed and predicted pre-cue response proportions in Correct and Errors facets. Errors contains four response categories; the legend is on the right.' width=100%} ::: ::: ::: {.notes} Error bars are ±1 participant-level SE. Correct uses a 0.5–0.9 scale; Errors uses 0–0.20. The model underpredicts other-distractor responses. Acknowledge this discrepancy before interpreting the filtering parameter. ::: ## Parameter estimates: Item, binding, and filtering {#interpret-the-extension-alongside-model-fit .smaller .m3-figure} [specify · fit · [evaluate]{.on}]{.track} ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](../data/figures/m3_complex_parameters.png){fig-alt='Pre-cue parameter medians and 95 percent credible intervals: a and c on a 0 to 6 activation scale, f on a 0 to 1 scale, colored blue, orange, and green.' width=70%} ::: ::: ::: {.small} Medians and 95% credible intervals. Filtering is shown on the 0–1 scale. ::: ::: {.notes} This fit uses only pre-cue responses. a and c describe item activation and context binding; f scales distractor activation relative to targets. The same f scales distractor item and binding contributions in the standard complex-span model. Interpret these estimates alongside the predictive check, which shows systematic underprediction of other-distractor responses. ::: ## Further reading and advanced use {.m3-reading-slide} :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="65%"} Frischkorn, G. T., & Li, C. <script>
  // htmlwidgets need to know to resize themselves when slides are shown/hidden.
  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current
  // slide changes (different for each slide format).
  (function () {
    // dispatch for htmlwidgets
    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });
    }

  })();
</script>
